chunks.content: [01:15] Today we are diving into pgvector HNSW indexes in PostgreSQL. Unlike IVFFlat, HNSW builds a multi-layer navigable small world graph that gives sub-10ms approximate nearest neighbor queries without requiring a training step.

[04:40] The main trade-off with HNSW is memory usage and index build time. As your EpisodeChunk table grows past a million 1536-dimensional vectors, the HNSW graph can exceed shared_buffers and slow down inserts.

[09:20] Pure semantic embeddings often miss exact identifiers like error codes, library names such as tsvector, or acronyms like RRF. Combining dense cosine similarity with PostgreSQL full-text search fixes those blind spots.
[02:05] When processing large audio files, workers crash or get OOM-killed. We use BullMQ with 3 attempts and exponential backoff starting at 2000ms so transient network blips recover automatically.

[07:30] To prevent duplicate work when a job retries, we record every stage in a JobStep table. Before running transcription or embeddings, the worker checks if that stepId is already marked completed.

[12:15] FFmpeg normalization runs in a separate Node media-worker container before handing off to the Python ai-worker via the ai-pipeline queue. Keeping media transcoding isolated protects the AI worker from CPU spikes.

[03:10] We switched transcription to the Azure Speech REST API with speaker diarization enabled for up to two speakers. Each recognized phrase returns an ISO-8601 offset that we format into [MM:SS] timestamps.
[08:50] Splitting transcripts purely by word count cuts right through sentences and speaker turns. Respecting line and sentence boundaries keeps each chunk self-contained for the LLM.
[05:00] Karpenter replaces traditional Cluster Autoscaler by provisioning right-sized EC2 spot instances in under 45 seconds based on pending pod resource requests.
[11:25] For serverless cold starts, keeping container images slim and lazy-loading SDK clients at request time rather than module import time cuts startup latency significantly.
[06:12] Enabling SQLite WAL mode (Write-Ahead Logging) allows concurrent readers while a single writer appends to the WAL file, eliminating most SQLITE_BUSY lock errors in read-heavy web apps.
[14:00] Litestream continuously streams SQLite WAL frames to S3 or Azure Blob Storage so you get point-in-time recovery without running a separate database server.
